newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrican mining industry stuck in the past - report.
newsitem.headline: SAfrican mining industry stuck in the past - report.

text.p: The South African mining industry, often cricitised for low pay and endemic violence, is stuck in a culture of the past that is proving too slow to change, a government-commissioned report said on Tuesday.
The report, released by the Department of Labour, is aimed at gathering information about conditions in South Africa's mining industry and making recommendation on improvements.

The survey said current working practises are a legacy of the racist apartheid era unsuitable to South Africa's fledgling democracy. They are also inefficient and prevent the South African industry from competing with global rivals.

"Perhaps the greatest obstacle to the restructuring of work consists in the resilience of a mining culture which has nurtured inefficient labour practises for the past hundred years," the report said.
South Africa's mines, long the backbone of the country's economy, rose to glory on the backs of hundreds of thousands of migrants from the countryside and neighbouring states.

The report said wages in the industry were still below the poverty line. The poorly-paid workers have also traditionally been housed in hostels, often segregated on ethnic lines, and the result has been frequent flare-ups of violence.

The most recent clashes hit a platinum mine northwest of Johannesburg earlier this month and killed 32 people. Fighting broke out at a squatter camp called Freedom Park near Wildebeesfontein mine after a Xhosa-speaking shopowner allegedly killed a Sotho man for stealing milk from his shop.

Tito Mboweni, minister of labour, laid the blame for such squatter camps squarely at the door of mining firms who sometimes pay workers a small living out allowance instead of providing housing. "The mining houses have continually tried to dodge this issue," he told a news conference.

The report said housing arrangements in the industry must change to prevent further bloodshed. The key to doing this is to replace the migrant labour system with a more stable workforce so family-based accommodation can be built.
"The provision of housing must be altered to meet the needs of a stabilised workforce," the report said.

However, the report warned that changes in the workforce, in particular large-scale retrenchments, must be conducted carefully to avoid social upheaval in many communities in South Africa and overseas that rely on wages sent home by miners.
"The men and women who paid the price of building the industry should not have to bear the costs for its restructuring," said Professor Eddie Webster, who oversaw the drawing up of the report.
The importance of the South African industry to the entire southern African region could not be overlooked, he added.
"For many of our neighbours the mining industry remains the centre of their economy," he said.
The report also criticised health and safety in the industry and called for adoption of basic internationl standards, with mining disasters still all too frequent in South Africa.
Last year a train at a Vaal Reefs' mine south-west of Johannesburg plunged into a shaft and hit a lift, killing 104 men. An inquiry found Vaal Reefs liable for the catastrophe.
